summary: The Sieve Email Filtering Language (RFC 5228) is used for filtering mail at final delivery. This document creates an IANA registry for Sieve actions, helping developers and extension writers track interactions between different extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail filter rules can do different actions. This document starts an official list of those actions so makers of add-ons can avoid clashes.

questions: what is the sieve actions registry
how do i register a sieve action
what does implicit keep mean in sieve
subtitle: A new IANA registry that lists every Sieve mail-filtering action and how it interacts with the others.

tldr.problem: Sieve has many extensions that can interact in complex ways, and there was no easy way to find all the actions they define, so extension writers and implementers struggled to foresee interactions.
tldr.mechanism: The document has IANA create a Sieve Actions registry, defines a registration template with fields such as capabilities and whether an action cancels the implicit keep, and fills it with the initial actions.
tldr.outcome: Developers get one place to look up Sieve actions and their interactions. The RFC adds no new security considerations and says the registry may improve specification and implementation quality.

today: RFC 9122 is a Proposed Standard from June 2023. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the Sieve Actions registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Sieve Email Filtering Language (RFC 5228) is described as a popular language for filtering email at final delivery. Its popularity produced many Sieve extensions that can interact with each other in complex ways.

There was no easy way to find all actions defined by Sieve extensions published in RFCs. That made it hard for extension writers and implementers to foresee interactions between actions. This document creates a registry of Sieve actions to fix that.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of people added new tricks to mail filters, and nobody had a full list. Now there is one.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
IANA has created the Sieve Actions registry. Actions from both RFCs and vendor-specific documentation may be registered, and this is encouraged. Each entry has these fields:

  • Name and Description of the action.
  • References: documents describing the action. Required for actions in RFCs, optional otherwise.
  • Capabilities: the Sieve capabilities associated with the action.
  • Action Interactions: interactions with other actions, if any (see Section 2.10.1 of RFC 5228).
  • Cancels Implicit Keep?: whether the action cancels the implicit keep (Section 2.10.2 of RFC 5228).
  • Can Use With IMAP Events?: whether it can be used with IMAP events in Sieve (RFC 6785).
  • Comments: optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is like a trading card with the same boxes to fill in: name, what it does, and what it plays well with.

sections.title: Registration Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure is Expert Review (RFC 8126). The designated expert only checks that the action name matches its documentation, that the description is accurate, that the correct documents are referenced, and that the list of relevant documents is as complete as possible.

The expert cannot reject a registration because of a personal dislike for the document defining an action, and should always err on the side of approving it, even if the documentation is incomplete. The same procedure is used to add a new reference or change the description of an existing entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper checks that the card is filled in correctly. The helper is not allowed to say no just because they do not like the idea.

sections.title: The Initial Registry Contents
sections.content:
The registry starts with these actions: addheader, addflag, convert, deleteheader, discard, enclose, ereject, extracttext, fileinto, keep, notify, redirect, reject, removeflag, replace, set, setflag and vacation. Each entry cites the RFCs that define it, such as RFC 5228 for discard and keep.

An Action Interactions value of N/A means no restriction on using the action with any other action, though implementers still need to read the specifications for surprising behaviors. The Comments field is left out of these entries because none have comments.
sections.plainLanguage: The first list has eighteen tricks, from throwing a message away to sending an automatic vacation reply.

sections.title: Notable Interactions
sections.content:
Several entries show why the registry is useful. addheader, deleteheader and convert alter the message, so all subsequent tests and actions apply to the altered message. For enclose and replace, this holds for everything except redirect.

reject and ereject are incompatible with vacation, and are typically not permitted with actions that cause delivery, such as keep, fileinto and redirect. For fileinto and redirect, use of :copy suppresses cancellation of the implicit keep.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tricks do not mix. You cannot both refuse a message and say you are on vacation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The sole purpose of the document is to create the registry, so it creates no new security considerations for Sieve implementations. The RFC says the registry might improve the quality of specifications and implementations, including security aspects, by helping people track interactions between actions.

For security considerations of a particular action, readers should see the RFCs referenced for it in the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A list does not make anything riskier. For the safety rules of one trick, read the paper that describes that trick.
